modules.label: Labor & Delivery
modules.summary: Labor has a shape and a set of decision points — knowing them ahead of time turns a scary unknown into a checklist.

lessons.title: Stage 1: Dilation
lessons.why: The longest stage by far — knowing that up front prevents a lot of unnecessary panic early on.
facts: Contractions dilate the cervix from 0 to 10cm.
The longest of the three stages — often 8–14 hours for a first baby.
Usually split into early labor (slower) and active labor (faster, more intense) phases.

lessons.title: Stage 2: Pushing and delivery
lessons.why: Shorter and more intense than Stage 1 — the part most people picture when they think of "labor."
facts: Begins once the cervix is fully dilated at 10cm.
Pushing and delivery of the baby.
Usually 20 minutes to a few hours.

lessons.title: Stage 3: Delivering the placenta
lessons.why: Often forgotten in birth-prep conversations, but it's still part of the process.
facts: Delivery of the placenta, after the baby is born.
Typically 5–30 minutes after birth.
Your care team will check that it's delivered completely, since retained fragments can cause bleeding.

lessons.title: Signs of true labor vs. Braxton Hicks
lessons.why: False alarms are common in the last weeks — this is how to tell the difference.
facts: True contractions get closer together, longer, and stronger over time; Braxton Hicks stay irregular and often ease with rest or hydration.
True labor pain doesn't go away with a position change; Braxton Hicks often do.
Other real signs: your water breaking, or a "bloody show" (mucus plug with light spotting).
lessons.mustRemember: Call your care team if contractions are 5 minutes apart, lasting 1 minute, for 1 hour ("5-1-1") — or immediately if your water breaks.

lessons.title: When to head to the hospital
lessons.why: Leaving too early or too late are both common regrets.
facts: Follow the 5-1-1 rule for first labors, but go sooner if your hospital is far or it's not your first baby.
Go immediately for: water breaking, heavy bleeding, reduced fetal movement, or severe unrelenting pain.
Call the hospital/clinic first — they may want you to come straight in rather than wait out contractions at home.

lessons.title: Pain relief: Epidural
lessons.why: The most common choice by far — worth understanding what it actually does and doesn't do.
facts: Regional anesthesia, delivered via a catheter in the lower back.
Doesn't fully remove sensation, but numbs most pain from the waist down.
Typically takes 10–20 minutes to place and take effect — worth requesting before pain is severe, not at the last minute.

lessons.title: Pain relief: Nitrous oxide (gas & air)
lessons.why: A lighter-touch option than an epidural, for when you want to stay more mobile and in control.
facts: Short-acting and self-administered through a mask or mouthpiece, breath by breath.
Wears off fast once you stop using it, with no lasting effect on baby.
Can be combined with other pain relief, or used on its own.

lessons.title: Pain relief: Non-medical options
lessons.why: Worth having in the mix even if you also want an epidural — many people use both.
facts: Breathing techniques to stay ahead of the pain rather than reacting to it.
Water immersion (a bath or shower) and movement/position changes.
Massage and counter-pressure from a birth partner, especially for lower-back pain.

lessons.title: The birth partner's real job
lessons.why: This is what actually helps versus what looks helpful in movies.
facts: Advocate: relay her wishes to staff when she can't easily speak for herself.
Track time: note contraction frequency and duration so you have real numbers when calling the hospital.
Stay calm and present — your steadiness is often more valuable than anything you say.

lessons.title: C-section basics
lessons.why: Roughly 1 in 3 births in Singapore involve a C-section — worth understanding even if unplanned.
facts: Can be planned (breech position, placenta previa, prior C-section) or unplanned (labor stalls, fetal distress).
Recovery is longer than vaginal birth — typically 4–6 weeks, with limits on lifting and driving.
A support partner is usually allowed in the room for both planned and emergency C-sections in Singapore.

modules.takeaway: You can't control how labor unfolds, but you can control being prepared — pack the hospital bag early, know your 5-1-1, and settle your pain-relief preferences and support plan in advance.

modules.label: Newborn Basics
modules.summary: Newborns need frequent, hands-on care in a few areas — none of it complicated once you know what's normal.

lessons.title: Newborn feeding cues
lessons.why: Newborns signal hunger well before crying — catching it early makes feeds calmer.
facts: Early cues: rooting (turning head, mouth open), sucking on hands, smacking lips.
Crying is a late cue — by then the baby is already distressed and harder to latch.
Expect 8–12 feeds per 24 hours in the first weeks, whether breast or bottle.

lessons.title: Umbilical cord stump care
lessons.why: Simple, but a common source of new-parent anxiety.
facts: Keep it dry and exposed to air — fold diapers below it, and stick to sponge baths until it falls off.
It typically falls off on its own within 1–3 weeks. Some blood-tinged discharge right before is normal.
Call your pediatrician if you see pus, redness spreading to the skin, or a foul smell.

lessons.title: Bathing a newborn
lessons.why: You don't need to (and shouldn't) bathe a newborn every day.
facts: 2–3 times a week is enough before the baby is mobile — daily bathing can dry out their skin.
Sponge baths only until the umbilical cord falls off.
Keep water lukewarm (around 37°C) and never leave the baby unattended, even for a second.
lessons.mustRemember: Never leave a baby alone in bath water — not even to grab a towel. Bring everything within arm's reach first.

lessons.title: Diapering essentials
lessons.why: You'll do this 8–10 times a day — worth doing efficiently.
facts: Change before or right after feeds, and immediately after a bowel movement.
For boys, point the penis downward before closing the diaper to avoid leaks upward.
Watch for diaper rash — treat early with a barrier cream and more frequent changes.

lessons.title: What's normal in the diaper
lessons.why: Poop changes fast in the first week, and again depending on how baby's fed — worth knowing what's expected.
facts: The first stools (meconium) are black and tarry, usually in the first 1–3 days.
Over the next few days it transitions through greenish-brown to a more typical color and texture.
Breastfed stool is usually looser, seedy, and mustard-yellow; formula-fed stool is typically firmer and tan-brown.
lessons.mustRemember: Call your pediatrician for hard, pellet-like stools with straining and no result, true diarrhea, or any blood in the stool.

modules.takeaway: Feeding cues, cord care, bathing, diapering, and poop all settle into a rhythm within the first couple of weeks — the learning curve is real but short.

modules.label: Crying & Soothing
modules.summary: Crying is communication, not danger — work the checklist first, then reach for the 5 S's.

lessons.title: The quick checklist before anything else
lessons.why: Most crying has a simple, fixable cause — check these before assuming something's wrong.
facts: Hungry — the most common cause, especially in the first weeks.
Tired, wet or soiled, too hot or too cold, or simply wants to be held.
Overstimulated — sometimes a quiet, dim room is the fix, not more input.

lessons.title: The 5 S's: the idea
lessons.why: Dr. Harvey Karp's "5 S's" recreate the womb environment and reliably trigger a newborn's calming reflex.
facts: Swaddle, side/stomach hold, shush, swing, and suck — five specific techniques, not a random list.
Each one mimics a condition in the womb: snugness, being held, constant whooshing noise, motion, sucking.
Try them together rather than one at a time — most parents find a combination works better than any single S alone.

media.caption: The 5 S's to Soothe Your Baby — Dr. Harvey Karp, Happiest Baby

lessons.title: S #1: Swaddle
lessons.why: Recreates the snugness of the womb and stops a baby's own startle reflex from waking them back up.
facts: Wrap snugly with arms in; leave room at the hips for legs to bend up and out, frog-style.
Snug at the chest, looser at the hips — swaddling the legs too tightly raises hip dysplasia risk.
Stop swaddling for sleep the moment baby shows signs of rolling — a swaddled roll is a suffocation risk.

media.caption: Swaddle Your Baby Like a Pro: Pediatrician Tips

lessons.title: S #2: Side or stomach hold
lessons.why: A different position and belly pressure than an upright cradle hold — often calms a baby a cradle hold doesn't.
facts: Hold baby on their side or stomach along your forearm, supporting the head and neck.
This is for soothing while awake and supervised only — never a sleep position.
Sleep must always be on the back, alone, in the crib (see Safe Sleep Basics) — this hold is just for calming.

lessons.title: S #3: Shush
lessons.why: Newborns just spent 9 months next to the loud whoosh of blood flow — near-silence is unfamiliar, not soothing.
facts: A loud, continuous "shhh" held right next to baby's ear — louder than most parents expect at first.
A white-noise machine or app works too, as long as it's loud and continuous rather than soft and intermittent.
Match the shush volume to how hard the baby is crying, then taper it down gradually as they calm.

lessons.title: S #4: Swing
lessons.why: Stillness is the least womb-like state — motion is what most reliably keeps the calming reflex switched on.
facts: Small, fast, rhythmic motion — a tight jiggle, not a big slow rock.
Always support the head and neck fully; the motion should never be a shake or a jerk.
Once baby is calm, the motion can be slowed down gradually rather than stopped abruptly.

lessons.title: S #5: Suck
lessons.why: Sucking triggers one of the strongest newborn calming reflexes, separate from actual hunger.
facts: A pacifier or a clean finger works if baby isn't due for a feed.
Offering the breast or bottle works too, if you're not trying to avoid comfort-feeding.
Often the most effective added last, once the other S's have already gotten baby partway calm.

lessons.title: Purple crying is real, and it's not your fault
lessons.why: Some crying has no fixable cause at all — knowing this in advance heads off a lot of self-blame.
facts: "Purple crying" is a normal stretch of unexplained, hard-to-soothe crying that peaks around 6 weeks.
It usually resolves on its own by 3–4 months, regardless of what soothing method you use.
It's named and taught specifically to prevent shaken baby syndrome — the crying is not a sign you're doing something wrong.
lessons.mustRemember: If nothing is working and you feel your own frustration rising, it's safe to put baby down in the crib and step away for a few minutes. Never shake a baby.

media.caption: The Period of PURPLE Crying — National Center on Shaken Baby Syndrome

modules.takeaway: If nothing is working after a real effort, it's safe to put baby down in the crib and step away for a few minutes. Never shake a baby.

modules.label: Sleep
modules.summary: Newborn sleep looks chaotic by adult standards — that's normal, not a sign anything's wrong.

lessons.title: How much newborns actually sleep
lessons.why: Knowing the real numbers ahead of time stops you from panicking over something that's completely normal.
facts: Newborns sleep 14–17 hours a day in total.
But rarely more than 2–4 hours at a single stretch, day or night.
This comes from their small stomachs and short sleep cycles — not something you can train away early on.

lessons.title: Fixing day/night confusion
lessons.why: Newborns are born with no sense of day and night — you have to help them learn it.
facts: Being more alert at night and sleepier by day is normal in the first weeks.
Bright light and activity during the day, dim and quiet at night, help reset the body clock.
It typically resolves within a few weeks as their circadian rhythm matures.

lessons.title: Starting a wind-down routine early
lessons.why: The specific routine matters less than starting the habit of one, consistently, from day one.
facts: A short, consistent wind-down (dim lights, swaddle, quiet) can start from week one.
Consistency matters more than the exact steps — babies respond to the pattern repeating.
It won't produce a predictable schedule yet, but it lays the groundwork for one later.

lessons.title: Sleep regressions
lessons.why: A sudden return to frequent night waking after things were going well usually isn't a problem to fix — it's a phase to get through.
facts: The best-known is the "4-month regression" — a real reorganization of sleep-cycle structure, not a decline.
It typically lasts 2–6 weeks: more night wakings, shorter naps, harder bedtimes.
Further bumps are common around 8–10 months and 12 months, usually tied to developmental leaps or teething.

lessons.title: Developmental leaps
lessons.why: A useful lens for the fussy stretches that don't have an obvious cause — most trace back to a leap, not something wrong.
facts: Many parents track these using a framework called "developmental leaps" (popularized as "Wonder Weeks") — periods of rapid perceptual/cognitive development, roughly around weeks 5, 8, 12, 19, 26, 37, and 46, though timing varies a lot by baby.
Each leap tends to have a fussy phase first — more crying, clinginess, disrupted sleep, eating less — followed by a noticeable new skill or awareness.
It's a popular parenting framework, not a strict medical schedule — useful as a reassuring lens for an otherwise unexplained fussy stretch, not something to plan life around precisely.

lessons.title: How naps evolve
lessons.why: There's no one "right" nap schedule — it shifts predictably as babies get older.
facts: Newborns nap in short, frequent bursts with no real pattern.
By about 4–5 months, most babies shift toward a more predictable 3-nap-a-day rhythm.
By around 6 months, many babies settle into 2–3 semi-predictable naps — consistency of wake windows matters more than clock time early on.

modules.takeaway: Expect fragmented, unpredictable sleep for months — focus on safety (see Safe Sleep Basics), not a schedule, for now.

modules.label: Postpartum
modules.summary: Postpartum recovery is a longer, more varied process than most people expect — physically and emotionally.

lessons.title: Vaginal bleeding (lochia)
lessons.why: One of the most visible parts of recovery, and one of the least talked about beforehand.
facts: Vaginal bleeding (lochia) can last 4–6 weeks.
It tapers over that time, from bright red, to brown, to yellow-white.
A sudden return to heavy bright-red bleeding after it's tapered is worth calling your care team about.

lessons.title: Overall physical recovery timeline
lessons.why: "Recovery" isn't a single day — it's a gradual process, longer than film montages suggest.
facts: Full physical recovery is closer to 6–8 weeks minimum.
Recovery after a C-section takes longer than after a vaginal birth, with added limits on lifting and driving.
The 6-week postpartum check is the usual point your care team formally clears you for normal activity.

lessons.title: Afterpains
lessons.why: An often-unexpected part of recovery — worth knowing in advance that it's normal.
facts: Afterpains are the uterus contracting back down to its pre-pregnancy size.
They're normal, not a sign something's wrong.
They're often stronger with each subsequent baby, and noticeable especially during breastfeeding.

lessons.title: Baby blues
lessons.why: Extremely common, and passes on its own — distinguishing it from PPD matters.
facts: Affects up to 80% of new mothers.
Mood swings, weepiness, and anxiety in the first 2 weeks after birth.
Resolves on its own, typically within 2 weeks, without treatment.

lessons.title: Postpartum depression (PPD)
lessons.why: One is expected and passes; PPD needs professional support — telling them apart matters.
facts: Lasts longer than 2 weeks and is more intense than baby blues — persistent sadness, hopelessness, difficulty bonding.
Treatable and common — it affects fathers/partners too, not just mothers.
Screening is available through your polyclinic or hospital.
lessons.mustRemember: If low mood lasts beyond 2 weeks, or includes thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, contact a doctor immediately — this is medical, not a personal failing.

lessons.title: Pelvic floor recovery
lessons.why: Often skipped in prep, but affects long-term comfort and health.
facts: Pelvic floor muscles are stretched by pregnancy and vaginal delivery, and weakened even after C-sections.
Gentle pelvic floor exercises can typically start within days postpartum, but check with your obstetrician first.
Singapore hospitals and polyclinics offer postnatal physiotherapy referrals — worth asking about at your 6-week check.

lessons.title: Sex and intimacy after birth
lessons.why: Timelines vary widely — this removes the guesswork.
facts: Most doctors advise waiting until after the 6-week postpartum check before resuming penetrative sex.
Hormonal changes (especially while breastfeeding) can reduce libido and cause vaginal dryness — this is temporary and normal.
Non-sexual intimacy and communication matter more in this window than most couples expect.

lessons.title: Building your support system now
lessons.why: The best time to arrange help is before you need it desperately.
facts: Decide in advance who's doing what in the first 2 weeks: meals, errands, night wake-ups, visitors.
If hiring a confinement nanny or postpartum doula, book 2–3 months ahead — good ones are fully booked early in Singapore.
Agree with your partner on a "tag out" signal for when either of you is overwhelmed, before you're in the moment.

modules.takeaway: If low mood lasts beyond 2 weeks, or includes thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, contact a doctor immediately — this is medical, not a personal failing.

modules.label: Logistics (SG)
modules.summary: A handful of Singapore-specific logistics have real deadlines — better handled ahead of time than in the fog of week one.

lessons.title: Hospital bag: for mum
lessons.why: Pack by week 36 — babies don't wait for your to-do list.
facts: ID/passport and insurance card.
Maternity pads and a nursing bra.
A comfortable going-home outfit and your phone charger.

lessons.title: Hospital bag: for baby
lessons.why: A short list, but easy to forget in the rush of everything else.
facts: A going-home outfit.
A swaddle or blanket.
A car seat, installed in the car beforehand — not something to figure out at discharge.

lessons.title: Hospital bag: for partner
lessons.why: Hospital stays involve a lot of waiting — pack for that, not just for the birth itself.
facts: Snacks and a change of clothes.
Entertainment for long stretches of waiting.
Cash/cards for parking and food.

lessons.title: Paternity & shared parental leave (2026 rules)
lessons.why: This changed recently — worth knowing the current numbers, not the ones from a few years ago.
facts: Fathers of Singapore-citizen children get 4 weeks of Government-Paid Paternity Leave (GPPL), mandatory since April 2025.
From 1 April 2026, an additional Shared Parental Leave (SPL) pool of 10 weeks is split between both parents (5 weeks each by default, reallocatable).
Combined with 16 weeks of maternity leave, eligible families can access up to 30 weeks of paid leave in baby's first year — leave must generally be used within 12 months of birth.

lessons.title: Registering the birth
lessons.why: There's a hard deadline most new parents don't know about.
facts: Births in Singapore must be registered within 42 days at the Registry of Births and Deaths (usually done at the hospital before discharge).
You'll need both parents' NRICs/passports and the marriage certificate (if applicable).
The birth certificate is required to open a CDA account and apply for Baby Bonus.
lessons.mustRemember: Register the birth within 42 days — most hospitals help you do this before discharge, so ask about it on admission.

lessons.title: Baby Bonus & CDA account
lessons.why: Free government money that requires you to actively apply for it.
facts: The Baby Bonus cash gift and Child Development Account (CDA) require an online application after the birth is registered.
The CDA is a co-savings account — government matches your contributions up to a cap, usable for approved childcare/medical expenses.
Apply promptly — some components have time-sensitive application windows.

lessons.title: Choosing a pediatrician
lessons.why: Better to decide before you're sleep-deprived and need one urgently.
facts: Ask your gynae or hospital for a referral, or check which pediatric clinics are near home for late-night visits.
Confirm which hospital they're affiliated with, in case of admission.
Newborns typically need checkups at 1 week, 1 month, and then at regular intervals — book the first one before discharge.

lessons.title: Insurance to sort before birth
lessons.why: Some policies need to be in place before the baby arrives to avoid pre-existing condition exclusions.
facts: MediShield Life covers newborns automatically from birth for Singapore citizens/PRs, but check if you want additional Integrated Shield Plan coverage.
Congenital conditions are sometimes excluded unless you apply for coverage within a set window after birth — check the exact deadline with your insurer.
Confirm what your hospital plan covers for delivery (ward class, complications, NICU stay) before you're admitted.

modules.takeaway: Register the birth within 42 days, and don't leave Baby Bonus/CDA or insurance applications for "later" — several of these have real deadlines that don't wait for you to feel ready.

modules.label: Gear & Shopping
modules.summary: You need less than the internet wants you to buy — this is the actual short list, by category.

lessons.title: Sleep
lessons.why: The one category where less genuinely is more — safe sleep needs almost nothing extra.
facts: A crib or bassinet with a firm, flat mattress — no other bedding needed (see Safe Sleep Basics).
Fitted sheets sized to the mattress, plus a few spares for the inevitable diaper blowouts.
A few swaddles or sleep sacks, sized for the first months.

lessons.title: Feeding
lessons.why: Worth having a little backup on hand regardless of how you plan to feed.
facts: Bottles and formula on hand, even if planning to exclusively breastfeed — good to have as backup.
A breast pump if breastfeeding and planning to return to work, or want others able to feed baby.
Burp cloths — more than you think you'll need.

lessons.title: Diapering
lessons.why: Easy to overbuy the wrong size here.
facts: Diapers in newborn size and size 1 — don't overbuy newborn size, most babies size out of it within weeks.
Wipes and a barrier/diaper rash cream.
A changing pad, wherever you'll actually be changing diapers most — doesn't need to be a dedicated table.

lessons.title: Bathing & skin
lessons.why: A short list — bathing a newborn doesn't need much (see Bathing a Newborn).
facts: A baby bathtub or a bath support for the sink or tub.
Mild, fragrance-free soap and shampoo made for babies.
Soft towels (hooded ones are convenient) and washcloths.

lessons.title: Clothing
lessons.why: Birth weight varies enough that exact sizing is a guessing game until baby arrives.
facts: A mix of newborn and 0–3 month sizes, since you won't know which fits best until birth.
Bodysuits/onesies are the workhorse item — buy more of these than anything else.
Prioritize easy front or zip openings over anything that has to go over the head.

lessons.title: Going out
lessons.why: The one category with a genuinely non-negotiable item in it.
facts: A car seat, installed and checked before the due date (see Car Seat Basics) — not optional gear.
A stroller that fits your actual daily life (stairs, public transport, car boot size) more than one that looks ideal in a showroom.
A baby carrier, for the stretches where you need both hands free.

modules.takeaway: Buy less than you think for anything labeled "newborn" — most of it gets outgrown within weeks. Prioritize the car seat, the sleep setup, and diapers; almost everything else can wait, be borrowed, or be bought after baby arrives.

modules.label: Safety
modules.summary: A handful of safety basics have the strongest evidence behind them — worth locking in before the due date, even if the rest of babyproofing can wait.

lessons.title: Safe sleep basics
lessons.why: This single set of guidelines has the biggest evidence base for reducing SIDS risk.
facts: Back to sleep, every sleep, for the first year.
Firm, flat mattress in the crib/bassinet — no pillows, blankets, bumpers, or soft toys.
Room-sharing (not bed-sharing) for at least the first 6 months is recommended.
lessons.mustRemember: Back, flat, bare crib — every single sleep, including naps.

lessons.title: Car seat basics
lessons.why: Most parents install it wrong the first time — worth checking properly.
facts: Rear-facing car seat is mandatory in Singapore for infants, in the back seat.
The seat should be installed with no more than 2.5cm of movement side to side when tugged at the base.
Many workshops and some hospitals in Singapore offer free car seat installation checks — worth booking one before week 36.

media.caption: Installing a Rear-facing Car Safety Seat — American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)

lessons.title: Infant CPR
lessons.why: A skill you hope to never use, but one course removes most of the panic if you ever do.
facts: Infant CPR differs meaningfully from adult/child CPR — hands-on training beats reading about it.
Singapore Red Cross and SGH/KKH often run short infant first aid courses for expecting parents.
Aim to complete a certified course before the due date, ideally with both parents attending together.

lessons.title: Infant choking response
lessons.why: A distinct skill from CPR — worth knowing the difference before you'd ever need either.
facts: Choking response differs meaningfully from CPR and from adult/child choking response — hands-on training beats reading about it.
Singapore Red Cross and SGH/KKH often run short infant first aid courses covering this alongside CPR.
Aim to complete a certified course before the due date, ideally with both parents attending together.

media.caption: Baby first aid: Choking — British Red Cross

lessons.title: Babyproofing: before birth
lessons.why: The one stretch of babyproofing worth finishing before baby actually arrives.
facts: Safe sleep setup in place (see Safe Sleep Basics).
Smoke detectors working, with fresh batteries.
Water heater temperature capped to avoid scalds.

lessons.title: Babyproofing: by 4–6 months
lessons.why: Timed to when rolling typically starts — worth having done just ahead of it, not right after.
facts: Outlet covers on accessible sockets.
Secure furniture that could tip if pulled or leaned on.
Remove small choking hazards from floor level.

lessons.title: Babyproofing: by 8–9 months
lessons.why: Timed to when crawling and pulling-up typically start.
facts: Stair gates at the top and bottom of any stairs.
Cabinet locks, especially anywhere cleaning products or medicine are stored.
Cord/blind safety and corner guards on sharp furniture.

modules.takeaway: Back, flat, bare crib every sleep, and get CPR/choking-response certified before the due date — these two are worth prioritizing over the rest of the babyproofing timeline.

modules.label: Health & Doctor Visits
modules.summary: A handful of newborn quirks look alarming but usually aren't — a few real warning signs are worth knowing cold.

lessons.title: The first-year vaccination schedule (SG)
lessons.why: Your pediatrician tracks this for you, but knowing the shape of it helps you ask the right questions.
facts: Hepatitis B: first dose soon after birth, with 2 more doses folded into the 6-in-1 vaccine.
6-in-1 (DTaP-IPV-Hib-HepB): given at 2, 4, and 6 months, with a booster at 18 months.
Pneumococcal (PCV13): given at 4, 6, and 12 months.
lessons.mustRemember: All National Childhood Immunisation Schedule (NCIS) vaccines are fully subsidised for Singapore Citizen children at polyclinics.

lessons.title: Fever in the first 3 months: not the same as later
lessons.why: The threshold for "call now" is much lower than most people expect at this age.
facts: Any rectal temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher in a baby under 3 months needs urgent medical evaluation — there's no "mild fever" category at this age.
This is because a young baby's immune system can't yet reliably fight off infection — what looks mild can be serious.
Call your pediatrician immediately; if you can't reach them within a few minutes, go straight to the emergency department.
lessons.mustRemember: Fever ≥38°C in a baby under 3 months means call now — don't wait it out.

lessons.title: Jaundice: normal vs. worrying
lessons.why: About 6 in 10 newborns get some jaundice — knowing the difference between routine and urgent matters.
facts: Jaundice (yellowing skin/eyes from bilirubin) affects about 60% of newborns, usually appearing 3–5 days after birth.
It typically resolves on its own within 2 weeks, without treatment.
Call your doctor if it worsens, spreads to the arms/legs/whites of the eyes, or baby is hard to wake, feeding poorly, or it lasts beyond 2 weeks.

lessons.title: Common skin and tummy quirks that usually aren't a problem
lessons.why: A few very normal newborn things look alarming the first time you see them.
facts: Cradle cap — scaly, oily patches on the scalp from maternal hormones. Harmless and painless, usually clears on its own within months.
Baby acne — small facial bumps, also hormone-driven. Harmless; no treatment needed beyond gentle cleansing.

Reflux/spit-up — very common in the first 3 months. Normal if baby still seems happy, hungry, and is gaining weight; get checked promptly if it looks like real vomiting or baby seems unwell, especially in the first month.

modules.takeaway: Trust your gut over the internet for most things — but fever ≥38°C in a baby under 3 months, or jaundice that's worsening or lasting past 2 weeks, means call now, not later.
